near_miss.lead: Seeing light as life: the Greek and Armenian partner passages
near_miss.why_not: Electra 349 asks whether a man remains alive; the Armenian witness explicitly quotes a psalm about seeing light through divine light. Norse pivot concerns burning land. No matching inherited collocation with demonstrably cognate paired terms; scriptural mediation is explicit in Armenian.

Norse mutilation and miraculous restoration concern the tongue literally. Lucretius discusses the development of human speech; Plautus personifies bodily faculties. Tongue cognacy alone does not establish a shared formula; no matched predicate or distinctive syntax.

Read surrounding captivity narrative and searched Greek sleep vocabulary. Iliad 10.3–4 and 10.25–26 likewise describe anxious sleeplessness, but use different predicates and imagery. Norse sleep/rest coordination has no matching slab partner. Initial sleep/eye query used a nonmatching eye ID and is not evidence of absence. The positive Greek results establish a common situation, not a distinctive inherited phrase.

anchors: xcl:MH_1_1_06_Yeghishe ed. page 942 - PDF page 422 (word id 44843) (w2/2)
near_miss.lead: Light of the eyes; restoration or loss of sight
near_miss.why_not: Read Lucretius 3.1025 and 6.1146 with context. The former describes death, the latter inflamed eyes during plague; Norse describes miraculous sight restored by washing. No shared governing verb or stable paired expression. Root search returned no additional Latin hits; a form search also found Cato 157.10 on treatment of weak sight, but that is a practical prescription, not evidence of an inherited formula.

Norse remark about the heart accompanies extraction of an arrow and death; Atharvavedic durhārd/hṛdayena belongs to a counter-sorcery curse. No shared evaluative adjective, construction or specific image beyond ordinary heart language.

near_miss.lead: Water sought or found at doors
near_miss.why_not: Greek subjects stand at the king’s doors demanding irrigation water; Norse blind man kneels and crawls at a house to obtain healing water. Cognate doors and water name independent physical circumstances, without matching syntax or a distinctive formula.

near_miss.lead: Brother and sister in sexual-reputation narratives
near_miss.why_not: Read Norse siblings and the ensuing accusation against a priest, Old Russian letter defending reputation, and Vedic Yama/Yami dialogue. Brother and sister are cognate terms, but their juxtaposition follows the family relationships. No recurrent paired construction: Vedic rhetorical questions, Russian conditional repudiation, and Norse narrative possession differ.

near_miss.why_not: Norse saint heals bodily injuries in a dream; Herodotean dreams predict death or royal succession. Sleep is cognate but appearing/seeing in sleep is ordinary dream narration, with no distinctive matched formula. Tongue references in the other partners do not improve the equation.

near_miss.lead: Washing and a remarkable healing bath
near_miss.why_not: Norse commands washing wounds with water used for the king’s body. Cato lists cleaning jars, while Herodotus describes a spring that leaves bathers oily. Related bathing vocabulary does not establish the same inherited phrase or ritual.

anchors: xcl:MH_1_2_13_Lazar_Parp ed. page 2344 - PDF page 144 (word id 51713) (w2/2)
near_miss.why_not: Searched snow/white roots, then Greek snow forms. Norse repeats the simile for sails, horses, bodies and a saint; Old High German hits include biblical translations. Iliad 10.437 compares horses with snow, but Greek leukoteros/chionos does not reproduce the Norse hvitr/snjór cognate pair. The Christian vision and natural colour comparison offer no sufficient inheritance argument. No cross-branch cognate formula found.

Norse sorrowful prayer, Vedic mental generation, and Sanskrit release of the heart’s knot do not share a predicate or metaphor. The Hittite calendrical birth omens are also incongruent. Heart vocabulary is insufficient.

near_miss.lead: Dream ladder standing up to heaven
near_miss.why_not: Context identifies a saint’s dream of ascent; the sexual Vedic partners result from the erroneous Finnr mapping. No matching inherited phrase. Christian ladder imagery is a much closer narrative explanation than these retrieved comparisons.

near_miss.lead: God and men as a totality
near_miss.why_not: Norse fear of neither God nor men and violation of God’s and men’s laws are Christian moral expressions. The slab partners do not reproduce their merism or syntax. An exploratory indexed man/God-root query returned no hits; this is not proof of corpus-wide absence, and no distinctive cross-branch formula was established.

near_miss.lead: Tearful appeal to a divine mother
near_miss.why_not: Norse tears accompany appeals to God, Olaf and Mary; Iliad 1.357 has Achilles weeping and his own divine mother hearing him, while 22.79 has Hector’s mother herself weeping. Cognate mother and tear are not the same collocation; the Norse lacks the Greek pour-tears construction. Christian intercession cannot be treated as inherited pagan wording merely from analogous roles.

near_miss.lead: Sun fails to shine and darkness arrives
near_miss.why_not: The Norse death scene explicitly compares the event to the creator’s death. Serbian passages describe sunset or dawn, and Sanskrit a battle at midday. Shared sun vocabulary and light/darkness are insufficient: no shared predicate, distinctive syntax or inherited eclipse formula. Christian imitation is stated in the Norse context.

Norse prisoner is literally bound with iron; Bhagavadgita describes liberation from rebirth. Bind cognacy is real, but the Greek partner lacks the figure and the Sanskrit metaphor does not match Norse lexical or syntactic structure beyond ordinary binding. The saint’s release miracle supplies its own Christian narrative context.

Russian handful expressions and Norse restoration of an injured finger share only bodily vocabulary and whole/healed semantics. No common action or construction; Russian text also has obvious OCR corruption.
Norse crippled woman has bent feet; Homer describes a fighter whose legs no longer hold firm. Physical weakness alone does not supply a distinctive inherited collocation.

near_miss.lead: Dogs pursuing a fugitive in wild country
near_miss.why_not: Norse pursuit uses trained dogs to recapture a slave. Irish speaker defends himself from wild dogs over a long period; chonaib altaib is dative plural of cú with the adjective wild. Same animal, but different action and social context, with no matched inherited wording.
